prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: מערכת שעות כיתת י'2 – סמסטר א' (language he, right-to-left: column 1 is on the RIGHT).
Grid: 6 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "ראשון" spans 1 col × 2 row; "שני" spans 1 col × 2 row; "שלישי" spans 1 col × 3 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "יום" · longest unbreakable word 36px · one-line width 36px
  col 2: header "שעה" · longest unbreakable word 42px · one-line width 78px
  col 3: header "מקצוע" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 56px
  col 4: header "מורה" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 60px
  col 5: header "חדר" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 67px
  col 6: header "הערות" · longest unbreakable word 57px · one-line width 619px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 629px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 628px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Reasonable balance and no broken words, but the notes column (the only genuinely long content) is squeezed to roughly 200px, so every row grows to 5–7 lines while time/subject/teacher/room sit half-empty. Rows no longer read as compact units."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"Notes are crushed to about 130px, forcing one long paragraph per row into 8–10 narrow lines, while room, teacher and subject columns carry large empty areas. The table becomes a tall stack of ragged text strips instead of a scannable schedule."},"C":{"grade":"good","why":"Slightly more width to notes than A and a tighter time column, so rows are shorter and the day/time/subject/teacher/room block stays readable. Still more whitespace in the middle columns than necessary and notes wrap more than they need to."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Notes get the dominant share (roughly 330px), collapsing the longest cell to 3–4 lines, while day, time, subject, teacher and room are sized to their content and stay intact. Notes get only moderate width, so the table is tall and hard to compare."}},"best":["D"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"Widths were estimated by eye from the renders; small differences between A and C could shift their relative ranking, and I cannot verify exact pixel sums against the 628px budget."}
